## Animations

### Formation of solitary waves

A pressure pulse in a gas whose density varies periodically in space
breaks up into a train of solitary waves instead of forming shocks.  The
upper plot shows energy and the lower plot shows density; the plotting
window moves along with the waves.  This is the behavior described in
Section 1.1 and shown in Figure 1, though the background density here
varies smoothly rather than in piecewise-constant layers.

{{< video movies/euler_solitary_train_formation.mp4 >}}

### Comparison of the models

The setup of Section 2.5.1 and Figure 4: a moderate-amplitude pressure
pulse, plotted in the material (Lagrangian) coordinate.  The solutions of
the Euler equations and the $p$-system are indistinguishable, and the
homogenized $p$-system agrees closely, with differences in wave position
growing slowly over time.

{{< video movies/compare_3.mp4 >}}

The same experiment, showing only the $p$-system and the homogenized
$p$-system:

{{< video movies/psystem_comparison.mp4 >}}

A larger pulse in a shorter, periodic domain, comparing the $p$-system and
the homogenized $p$-system.  The pulse splits into left- and right-going
parts that wrap around the domain and meet again.  The agreement is less
close than for the smaller pulse above, and small-scale oscillations
appear in the $p$-system solution.

{{< video movies/psystem_homog.mp4 >}}

### Shock tube problems

These are the shock-tube-like problems of Section 4.1 (Figures 10 and 11):
a smoothed step in pressure, from a higher value $p_\ell$ on the left to 1
on the right, in a gas with periodically varying density.  The measurements
in the paper suggest that shocks form for $p_\ell \ge 2$ and not, or only
very weak ones, for smaller values.
